provisions_triggered.name: Due Process / Law of the Land

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Due Process Clause requires a State to support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence before it may permanently terminate the rights of parents in their natural child, so New York's fair-preponderance standard was unconstitutional.
key_cases.relevance: Santosky supplies the constitutional standard of proof that 33 V.S.A. ch. 53 termination proceedings must meet, and Vermont courts apply clear and convincing evidence at termination for exactly this reason.
key_cases.quote: The fundamental liberty interest of natural parents in the care, custody, and management of their child does not evaporate simply because they have not been model parents

key_cases.case_name: Lassiter v. Department of Social Servs. of Durham Cty.
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Constitution does not require appointment of counsel for indigent parents in every termination proceeding; the trial court decides case by case, subject to appellate review, and no error occurred on these facts.
key_cases.relevance: Lassiter is the federal floor for counsel at termination; Vermont exceeds it by statute (13 V.S.A. § 5232(3)), as In re C.B. and In re L.H. confirm, so a Vermont parent's counsel claim rests on the statute rather than on Lassiter alone.
key_cases.quote: leave the decision whether due process calls for the appointment of counsel for indigent parents in termination proceedings to be answered in the first instance by the trial court

key_cases.holding: Termination based in part on a father's extended pretrial incarceration was affirmed, because the court must assess individually how the incarceration, pretrial or not, affects that child's best interests rather than treat incarceration as an automatic ground.
key_cases.relevance: M.W. is Vermont's leading authority on terminating the rights of an incarcerated parent and forbids treating incarceration itself as dispositive.
key_cases.quote: Our statutory imperative requires the family court to review the individual circumstances of each child to determine how a parent's incarceration—whether pretrial or not— affects the child's best interests.

key_cases.holding: Termination was affirmed; a reasonable-efforts finding is a separate determination from the best-interests inquiry and is not a precondition to terminating parental rights, although the level of assistance given to parents remains relevant to whether they can resume parenting in a reasonable time.
key_cases.relevance: It is the controlling Vermont rule that a deficient reasonable-efforts record does not by itself defeat a termination petition.
key_cases.quote: the court is not required to find DCF made reasonable efforts as a prerequisite to termination

key_cases.case_name: In re L.H., L.H. and L.H., Juveniles
key_cases.holding: Termination orders were reversed and remanded for a new hearing because the lawyer who had represented the children then represented the State in the same matter, creating an unwaived conflict of interest that prejudiced the parents.
key_cases.relevance: L.H. holds that a termination judgment cannot stand where the State's lawyer previously represented the children in the same case.
key_cases.quote: we conclude that a conflict of interest by the State's counsel compromised the proceedings

key_cases.holding: The family court properly refused to vacate a termination order: 33 V.S.A. § 5113(b) does not reach termination orders even while an appeal is pending, and relief under § 5113(a) and Rule 60 was within the court's discretion to deny.
key_cases.relevance: C.L. is the controlling Vermont rule on the finality of a termination order and forecloses reopening it on changed circumstances.
key_cases.quote: we again reaffirm that § 5113(b) does not apply to a termination order, even if that order is currently the subject of an appeal

key_cases.holding: Denial of the mother's motion to modify and vacate a termination order was affirmed; the Court held that although the State's initial burden to terminate residual parental rights is clear and convincing evidence, a parent moving under 33 V.S.A. § 659(a) to modify or vacate that order need show changed circumstances only by a preponderance, absent an intervening adoption.
key_cases.relevance: T.E. is the Vermont source of the clear-and-convincing standard the State must satisfy to sever the parent-child relationship permanently, and it also fixes the lesser burden a parent bears when later moving to modify or vacate that termination order.
key_cases.quote: It is settled law that a state's initial burden of proof in seeking to terminate residual parental rights is by clear and convincing evidence.

key_cases.holding: Termination of the father's residual parental rights was affirmed, but the Court held that the most critical best-interests factor — whether the parent will be able to resume parental duties within a reasonable period of time — is forward-looking, and that parents must be judged on their conduct rather than on psychological test results.
key_cases.relevance: B.M. supplies Vermont's substantive termination analysis, which the rest of this layer lacked: the two-step changed-circumstances-then-best-interests framework, the stagnation test, and the requirement that the court assess the parent's prospective ability instead of treating an earlier period as dispositive.
key_cases.quote: the inquiry required by § 5540(3), which we have repeatedly emphasized as the most critical factor in a termination-of-parental-rights case, is forward-looking
